# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

<!-- OWNER: slice 2 (data description), slice 6 (final polish). -->

This report documents the investigation of a network capture that contains DNS tunneling, and the development of an anomaly detector that separates the malicious DNS queries from benign ones. The work was done for the course JM2030 Cybersecurity as Case 1 of the final project, with Isolation Forest [@liu2008isolation] as detection technique. Tactics and techniques follow the MITRE ATT&CK taxonomy [@attack].

**Data.** We received two artefacts: `case1.pcap`, a raw capture of DNS traffic, and `dns.log`, the DNS transaction log extracted from the same traffic with the Zeek network monitor [@zeek-dns]. The PCAP was used for manual inspection, the log for feature extraction. TODO (slice 2): number of packets and log rows, capture period, number of client hosts, number of distinct queried domains.

**Approach.** First we studied normal DNS behaviour and located the incident by hand in the PCAP. The result is a labelled ground truth, which allows proper metrics. Next we derived features that capture how DNS tunneling has to look on the wire, trained an Isolation Forest on them, and evaluated the detections against the ground truth, with a closer look at false positives and false negatives.

**Outline.** @sec-attack-investigation describes the protocol, the incident and the attack mechanics. @sec-detection describes features, model and evaluation. @sec-mitigation covers prevention and response, @sec-discussion discusses lessons and alternatives, and @sec-conclusion concludes. Indicators of compromise are listed in Appendix A.

## Protocols and Mechanics {#sec-protocols}

<!-- OWNER: slice 2. Add a protocol diagram (client, recursive resolver, authoritative name server). -->

DNS translates names into data such as IP addresses. A client sends a query to a recursive resolver, which, if the answer is not cached, walks the hierarchy from the root through the top-level domain to the authoritative name server of the queried zone [@rfc1035]. A query carries a name made of labels separated by dots, a type (`A`, `AAAA`, `MX`, `TXT`, `CNAME`, `NULL`, and others) and a class. The standard limits a label to 63 bytes and a full name to 255 bytes [@rfc1035]. DNS is typically allowed through firewalls because almost every network depends on it.

**Why this makes tunneling possible.** The name in a query is chosen by the sender, and an attacker who controls the authoritative name server for a domain receives every query for any subdomain of it. Data can therefore be encoded into the subdomain labels of the outgoing query and returned in the answer (for example in a `TXT` record). The resolver in the victim network relays the traffic without the attacker ever contacting the victim directly. This is what makes DNS a channel for command and control and for exfiltration [@farnham2013].

**Zeek `dns.log`.** One row per DNS transaction, with among others the timestamp, the source and destination address and port, the transaction id, the queried name (`query`), the type (`qtype_name`), the response code (`rcode_name`), the answers and the TTLs [@zeek-dns]. ## Attack Mechanics {#sec-mechanics}

<!-- OWNER: slice 6, with evidence from slices 1, 2 and 3. Each row must be backed by the data, not only literature. -->

Data hidden in query names forces the traffic to show certain properties, regardless of the tool used. These are the candidate core characteristics. The cells below are the hypothesis from the literature; slices 1 to 3 confirm or refute each with numbers from our data before the final version.

| Characteristic | Specificity | Benign overlap | Evasion difficulty | Automatable | Stage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long query names, long labels (payload in the name) | TODO | CDN and tracking domains also use long names | Attacker can shorten, but throughput drops | Yes, trivial | Exfiltration, C2 |
| High entropy of subdomain labels (encoded data) | TODO | Hash-like names (CDN, DNSSEC, mail) | Lower entropy encodings exist, at the cost of capacity | Yes | Exfiltration, C2 |
| Many unique subdomains under one parent domain | TODO | Some legitimate services (CDN, blocklists) | Hard: every payload chunk needs a unique name to avoid caching | Yes, needs a time window | Exfiltration, C2 |
| Uncommon record types (`TXT`, `NULL`, `CNAME` heavy) | TODO | `TXT` is used for SPF and verification | Medium | Yes | C2 |
| High and regular query rate to one domain | TODO | Busy legitimate services | Attacker can throttle, at the cost of speed | Yes, needs a time window | Exfiltration, C2 |
| High share of `NXDOMAIN` or unusual response sizes | TODO | Typos, blocklists | Medium | Yes | C2 |

# Detection Method Development and Evaluation {#sec-detection}

<!-- OWNER: slices 3, 4, 5. -->

The detection method is an unsupervised outlier detector over features derived from the characteristics in @tbl-characteristics. The chosen technique is Isolation Forest, explained in @sec-method-1. The ground truth from @sec-incident is not used for training. It is used only to evaluate.

## Features {#sec-features}

<!-- OWNER: slice 3. -->

TODO (slice 3): confirm this table against the implemented code.

| Feature | Level | What it measures | Targets characteristic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Query length | query | total length of the name | long names |
| Longest label length | query | longest label in the name | long labels |
| Label count | query | number of labels | structured payload |
| Shannon entropy of subdomain | query | randomness of the labels | encoded data |
| Digit and uppercase ratio | query | share of digits and uppercase characters | encoded data |
| Record type | query | encoded `qtype_name` | uncommon types |
| Unique subdomains per parent domain per window | window | count of distinct subdomains | many unique subdomains |
| Queries per parent domain per window | window | query rate | high rate |
| `NXDOMAIN` ratio per host per window | window | share of failed lookups | failed lookups |

: Features derived from `dns.log` {#tbl-features}

## Detection Method 1: Isolation Forest {#sec-method-1}

<!-- OWNER: slice 4. -->

Isolation Forest isolates observations by randomly picking a feature and a split value. Anomalies are few and different, so they end up isolated after fewer splits than normal points. The anomaly score is derived from the average path length over an ensemble of random trees [@liu2008isolation]. We use the implementation in scikit-learn [@scikit-learn].

This fits the incident for four reasons: it scales to a large log, it needs no feature scaling, it copes with mixed features such as counts, ratios and lengths, and it does not need labelled attacks to train. Its weakness is the `contamination` parameter, which sets how many points are flagged. If tunnel traffic is a large share of all rows, the assumption "anomalies are few" weakens. We therefore report the share of malicious rows in our data and evaluate across a range of contamination values.
